title: THE SON JACOB LOVED TOO MUCH
paragraphs: THE SON JACOB LOVED TOO MUCH
The Coat, The Pit, The Palace, and the Scandalous Grace That Rewrote Everything
It begins with a father who loved one son differently than the others.
A love so obvious it became a wound.
A preference so visible it ignited hatred.
A family so broken that murder felt reasonable.

And yet somehow, through jealousy, betrayal, slavery, false accusations, prison walls, political corruption, famine, and tears that lasted decades, God was quietly writing one of the greatest redemption stories ever recorded.
Not because the people were righteous.
But because grace is stronger than scandal.
That is the story of Joseph.
And perhaps, if we are honest, it is also our story.
The first time Scripture introduces Joseph's family dynamics, it does not hide the dysfunction.
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children.”

וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אָהַב אֶת־יוֹסֵף
VeYisra'el ahav et-Yosef
The word אָהַב (ahav) means affection, attachment, devotion, deep love.
There is nothing wrong with love.
The visible symbol of that favoritism became the famous coat.
Traditionally translated as "coat of many colors," though scholars suggest it may describe a richly ornamented robe associated with distinction and status.
Every time Joseph wore it, his brothers saw what they believed they lacked.
Every family gathering became a battlefield.
Someone else's blessing starts feeling like your rejection.
Someone else's favor starts feeling like your abandonment.
Someone else's success starts feeling like your failure.
The brothers looked at Joseph and saw what they thought God had withheld from them.
Many people are doing the same thing today.
Comparison is one of the fastest ways to poison gratitude.
The brothers did not realize that Joseph's coat would not protect him from suffering.
The blessing they envied would eventually carry him through unimaginable pain.
Because what looks like favor from a distance often comes with a hidden cost.
Joseph's dreams only intensified the tension.
Genesis records Joseph sharing prophetic dreams that appeared to place him above his family.
Whether youthful immaturity or simple honesty, the result was explosive.
His brothers could no longer hear him without anger.
Eventually they saw him approaching from afar.
The people who shared his childhood.
The people who shared his blood.
The people who knew his laugh.
The people who knew his voice.
Sometimes the deepest wounds do not come from enemies.
They come from people whose names are already in our hearts.
Instead of killing him, they stripped him of his robe and threw him into a pit.
The place between promise and fulfillment.
The pit where God's promises seem impossible.
What Joseph could not see from the bottom of that pit was that God was already moving above it.
His brothers sold him into slavery.
Yet even there, God had not abandoned him.
One of the most repeated phrases in Joseph's story appears in Genesis 39.
Not when he reached the palace.
While he was forgotten in prison.
God's presence was not dependent upon Joseph's circumstances.
Neither is His presence dependent upon yours.
Some readers need to hear that again.
God being with you does not mean life will be easy.
It means you will not face it alone.
Joseph's story then takes another devastating turn.
At least from a human perspective.
Have you ever obeyed God and watched your situation get worse?
Many believers secretly struggle with that question.
They assume obedience should always produce immediate rewards.
Sometimes obedience leads through prison before it leads to promotion.
Sometimes faithfulness is tested in darkness before it is celebrated in light.
The prisoner became an interpreter of dreams.
The ruler became second only to Pharaoh himself.
What no human could orchestrate, God accomplished through providence.
The Hebrew concept often demonstrated throughout Genesis is that God remains sovereign even when He seems silent.
God was writing a story larger than Joseph could imagine.
Then came the moment that changes everything.
Standing before the very brother they had destroyed.
If anyone had a human reason to seek revenge, it was Joseph.
After revealing his identity, Joseph said:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”

אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה
וֵאלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה

Atem chashavtem alai ra'ah
VeElohim chashavah letovah
“You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good.”
Notice Joseph does not deny evil.
He does not call evil good.
He does not pretend betrayal never happened.
This is one of the deepest theological truths in all Scripture.
But He is so powerful that even human rebellion cannot stop His purposes.
The greatest evil in human history became the greatest display of divine love.
When Jesus was crucified, men intended death.
When religious leaders plotted, God was redeeming.
When soldiers nailed Him to wood, grace was opening heaven.
The Greek word Jesus cried from the cross in John 19:30 was:
The scandal of human sin met the overwhelming grace of God.
That is why Joseph's story ultimately points beyond Joseph.
Jesus was betrayed by His own disciple.
Joseph forgave those who wounded him.
Jesus saves souls from eternal death.
The son Jacob loved too much became a shadow of the Son the Father loves perfectly.
Not because Jesus was favored unfairly.
But because He alone is perfectly worthy.
And through Him, astonishingly, we become beloved too.
Not that we performed well enough.
But that Jesus entered our pit, carried our shame, bore our scandal, paid our debt, defeated death, and offers grace freely.
Perhaps that is why Joseph's story still grips hearts thousands of years later.
Because somewhere inside, we recognize ourselves.
Yet in every chapter, God remains the same.
Still rewriting stories that seem beyond repair.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting in your own pit.
Maybe the future feels buried beneath darkness.
The pit is not the end.
The prison is not the end.
The betrayal is not the end.
Because Jesus is still rewriting stories.
And if He can transform a pit into a palace, a cross into salvation, and a scandal into grace, He can rewrite your story too.
Which part of Joseph's story feels most like your life right now?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Your share could become the reminder that God has not abandoned them.
Sometimes one story can open a door that years of arguments never could.
One day you may discover that the chapter you begged God to remove became the chapter He used to save someone else.
